meta.title: Who really said "Do not dwell in the past, do not dream of the future"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: No literal translation — Fake Buddha Quotes reads it as a loose, unnumbered rendition of Dhammapada 348, traced to The Teaching of Buddha: The Buddhist Bible (1934), a Japanese anthology's 'Sacred Aphorisms'. The first two clauses are fair; the third swaps in 'concentrate the mind on the present moment'.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Do not dwell in the past, do not dream of the future'?
meta.ogDescription: Traced to a 1934 Japanese Buddhist anthology, not the Pali canon — though it reads as a loose rendition of Dhammapada 348. The first two clauses are fair; the third distorts the verse, trading non-clinging for a grip on the present.

answer.label: Not canonical — a 1934 anthology’s aphorism
answer.sourceLine: No Pali original. The wording is traced to The Teaching of Buddha: The Buddhist Bible (1934), published by the Federation of All Young Buddhist Associations of Japan, where it sits in a section headed ‘Sacred Aphorisms’ — that is, compiled and composed sayings, not translated scripture. The nearest canonical text is Dhammapada verse 348, and the interesting thing is where the two part company: the first two clauses are a reasonable poetic gloss, and the third one quietly distorts it, trading the verse’s non-clinging for a grip on the present.

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: No verse reads it verbatim — read as a loose, unnumbered rendition of Dhammapada 348
The Teaching of Buddha: The Buddhist Bible (1934), Japan
Dhammapada 348; compare also the Bhaddekaratta Sutta

source.excerpt: Give up what is before, give up what is behind, give up what is in the middle, when thou goest to the other shore of existence; if thy mind is altogether free, thou wilt not again enter into birth and decay.
trail: Start with the canon. Dhammapada 348 is quoted above in Max Müller’s 1881 translation, and the shape is unmistakably related: before, behind, and — crucially — in the middle. The Bhaddekaratta Sutta of the Majjhima Nikaya makes the same move at length: do not chase the past, do not place expectations on the future read verse 348 free ↗.

Now read the third clause. The verse says give up what is in the middle. The quotation says concentrate the mind on the present moment. That is not a paraphrase; it is a substitution, and Bodhipaksa calls it a significant distortion — the verse’s point, that nothing is to be clung to, gets lost. A present-focused teaching does exist in the canon (the Arañña Sutta: ‘they do not mourn for the past, they do not yearn for the future, they live on the present’), so the line is not alien to Buddhism — the objection is the lost note of non-clinging, not the presence of the present Bodhipaksa’s reading ↗.

The wording itself is traced to The Teaching of Buddha: The Buddhist Bible, published in Japan in 1934 by the Federation of All Young Buddhist Associations, in a section of ‘Sacred Aphorisms’. That is the same family of Japanese compilation that gave English readers several other famous non-canonical ‘Buddha’ lines — useful books, widely distributed, and repeatedly mistaken for primary sources.
source.excerptNote: Müller’s 1881 English. Read the three clauses in order and the modern quotation’s edit is impossible to miss: the verse gives up the past, gives up the future, and then gives up the present too. It is not recommending that you live in the now. It is recommending that you stop holding on to anything at all, which is a much less comfortable piece of advice.

source.rightsNote: The excerpt is safe: Müller’s 1881 Dhammapada is public domain worldwide, which is why we quote it rather than a modern translation. The quotation on this page is a different object — twentieth-century anthology prose whose text belongs to its publisher, and which we therefore do not present as free ancient material. Quote verse 348 as much as you like; quote the aphorism with attribution to the anthology, not to the Buddha. This is not legal advice.
source.useLine: Rights uncertain. This wording is 1934 anthology prose, not ancient public-domain text. Quote Dhammapada 348 (Müller, 1881) freely; for the aphorism itself, attribute the anthology and check with the publisher before commercial reuse.

author.name: Gautama Buddha
author.heading: Why it gets pinned on the Buddha
author.metaLine: c. 5th century BCE · founder of Buddhism · northern India
author.bio: Siddhartha Gautama, the Buddha, taught in northern India around the fifth century BCE, and the past-future-present structure really is his: the Bhaddekaratta Sutta and Dhammapada 348 both run it. That genuine resemblance is why this line passes inspection so easily — it is not a random invention but a familiar cadence with one word swapped. The swap happens to be the word that carries the doctrine, which is what makes it worth a page rather than a shrug.

misattribution.heading: The attribution problem
misattribution.intro: This is not a wild invention. It is a near-miss, which is a more interesting failure: two thirds of it is a fair rendering of a real verse, and the last third silently swaps the teaching for a more marketable one.

items.why: Fake Buddha Quotes reads the line as a loose, unnumbered rendition of Dhammapada 348 — the 1934 book’s ‘Sacred Aphorisms’ are recognisable Dhammapada renderings, just unnumbered and hard to pin to a verse. It is composed English rather than a verse-for-verse translation, with the third clause substituted.
‘Do not dwell in the past, do not dream of the future’ genuinely does capture Dhammapada 348 and the Bhaddekaratta Sutta’s warning against chasing what is gone and expecting what has not arrived.

Verse 348 asks you to give up what is in the middle too — the present included — while ‘concentrate the mind on the present moment’ asks you to hold it. Bodhipaksa calls this a significant distortion in which the point, non-clinging, gets lost. The canon is not actually silent on the present — the Arañña Sutta praises those who ‘live on the present’ — so what drops out here is release, not the moment the reading ↗.

The Teaching of Buddha: The Buddhist Bible mixes translated material with composed and compiled sayings. It is a fine book that was never claiming to be the canon — readers made that leap on its behalf, and hotel-drawer distribution did the rest.

Several of the most-quoted ‘Buddha’ lines in English — including the candles-and-happiness one — trace back to this family of twentieth-century Japanese anthologies rather than to any translator of Pali. If a line feels Buddhist but has no verse number, that is usually where to look first.

misattribution.truthLine: Not canonical. Traced to a 1934 Japanese anthology’s ‘Sacred Aphorisms’ — and its third clause distorts Dhammapada 348, which asks you to give up the present too the trace ↗.

context.heading: Why it resonates
lead: It is the founding sentence of the entire modern mindfulness industry, and it is doing something very shrewd: it names the two ways a mind escapes the present, then hands you a single, achievable instruction. Anyone who has lain awake rerunning an argument recognises the first clause immediately.
That is also why the edited third clause survives so well. ‘Concentrate on the present moment’ is an app, a course, a practice you can be good at. ‘Give up the present too’ is not a product.
detailsBody: Dhammapada 348, Müller 1881: give up what is before, what is behind, and what is in the middle.
The third item is the point. The verse is about crossing to the other shore with a mind that is holding nothing.
The Bhaddekaratta Sutta makes the same case at length: do not chase the past, do not place expectations on the future, see clearly whatever quality is present.
Seeing clearly is not the same as concentrating on. One is release; the other is a grip.
The quotation is a fine piece of advice. It just is not this teaching, and it is not a quotation.
context.pull: The verse gives up the present too. That part never makes the poster.
